title: ISC2 Certified Secure Software Lifecycle Professional (CSSLP)

nodes.title: Part 1: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Part 1. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: A backend microservice is intended only to read customer records to render a support UI, but it is provisioned with a database role that also grants row-delete, schema-alter, and full-table export rights it never uses. An attacker who later compromises the service is therefore able to mass-export the entire customer database. Which core secure-design principle was violated?
flashcards.back: Least privilege requires that every subject (user, process, service) be granted the minimum permissions strictly necessary to perform its authorised function. Handing a read-only support component delete and export rights it never exercises directly violates that principle and is what turned a service compromise into a mass data breach. Separation of duties is about splitting one process across multiple actors (for example, request vs approval) so that no single actor can commit fraud alone — it does not describe over-broad permissions given to one identity. Defense in depth would call for additional layers (network segmentation, DLP, query anomaly detection) around the database, but the root design defect here is the identity's excess authority, not missing layers. Fail-secure defaults describe how a control should behave when it fails (default-deny) rather than the size of the authority the control granted in the first place.

flashcards.front: A security programme manager wants to adopt a mature, publicly documented framework whose primary value is to measure the current state of software-security activities across the organisation by observing what dozens of other real firms actually do, so leadership can benchmark against peers and plan year-on-year improvement. Which framework best fits this need?
flashcards.back: BSIMM is explicitly a descriptive model: its authors visit member firms, record which of ~120 activities they actually perform, and publish the aggregate so any member can benchmark itself against the observed distribution — exactly the peer-benchmark use case in the stem. SAMM is prescriptive-plus-self-assessment: it defines target activities and asks the organisation to score itself, without collecting data from other firms. Microsoft SDL is a prescriptive internal-Microsoft process describing what activities to perform in each SDLC phase, not a benchmark. ISO/IEC 27034 is a standards-track framework that specifies an Application Security Life Cycle and reusable Application Security Controls; it too is prescriptive rather than an observational benchmark.

flashcards.front: During requirements analysis for a new online-banking feature a security architect wants to write formal artefacts that describe how a hostile actor could try to interact with the system, so that counter-requirements (validation, rate limits, monitoring) can be derived alongside the normal user stories before any code is written. Which artefact is the architect producing?
flashcards.back: Misuse cases (Sindre and Opdahl, sometimes called abuse cases by McDermott and Fox) are the requirements-phase technique in which a use case is inverted: the actor becomes a malicious actor and the flow describes how the misuse is attempted, so the team can add mitigation requirements to the specification. Data-flow diagrams are the input to threat-modelling techniques like STRIDE, but they describe structure rather than an attacker's storyline. Security regression tests belong to the testing phase, long after requirements are frozen. Non-functional requirements capture quality attributes such as availability and performance; they do not describe an attacker's goals or actions.

flashcards.front: A design team is classifying a threat in which an attacker replays a captured session cookie against a web application because the cookie is not bound to a short-lived nonce or client fingerprint, allowing the attacker to impersonate a legitimate user for the rest of the session lifetime. In the STRIDE threat-model taxonomy, which category best describes this threat?
flashcards.back: Replaying a stolen session cookie lets the attacker act under another user's identity, which is the definition of the Spoofing identity category in STRIDE. Tampering would apply if the attacker modified the cookie's contents (for example, elevating a role claim) rather than presenting a legitimate but stolen cookie unchanged. Repudiation covers gaps in auditability that let a user later deny actions they performed; it does not describe presenting someone else's credentials. Information disclosure covers unintended read-side exposure of data (verbose errors, directory listing, insecure S3 buckets), not identity assumption.

questions.q: A backend microservice is intended only to read customer records to render a support UI, but it is provisioned with a database role that also grants row-delete, schema-alter, and full-table export rights it never uses. An attacker who later compromises the service is therefore able to mass-export the entire customer database. Which core secure-design principle was violated?
choices: Separation of duties — no single role should combine incompatible responsibilities such as initiating and approving the same transaction.
Least privilege — the service should be granted only the exact permissions it needs to perform its intended task, and no more.
Defense in depth — multiple independent controls should be layered so that failure of one control does not defeat the whole system.
Fail-secure defaults — when a control fails, it should default to denying access rather than allowing it.
questions.explanation: Least privilege requires that every subject (user, process, service) be granted the minimum permissions strictly necessary to perform its authorised function. Handing a read-only support component delete and export rights it never exercises directly violates that principle and is what turned a service compromise into a mass data breach. Defense in depth would call for additional layers (network segmentation, DLP, query anomaly detection) around the database, but the root design defect here is the identity's excess authority, not missing layers. Fail-secure defaults describe how a control should behave when it fails (default-deny) rather than the size of the authority the control granted in the first place.

questions.q: A security programme manager wants to adopt a mature, publicly documented framework whose primary value is to measure the current state of software-security activities across the organisation by observing what dozens of other real firms actually do, so leadership can benchmark against peers and plan year-on-year improvement. Which framework best fits this need?
choices: Microsoft Security Development Lifecycle (SDL) — a prescriptive, phase-by-phase set of mandatory security activities that Microsoft applies to its internal engineering projects.
OWASP SAMM — a self-assessment maturity model organised into business functions and security practices, each scored on a fixed 0-to-3 scale.
ISO/IEC 27034 — an international standard that defines an Application Security Life Cycle and a catalogue of Application Security Controls to be tailored by the organisation.
BSIMM (Building Security In Maturity Model) — a descriptive study that observes and quantifies what other real firms already do, so members can benchmark themselves against those observed activities.
questions.explanation: BSIMM is explicitly a descriptive model: its authors visit member firms, record which of ~120 activities they actually perform, and publish the aggregate so any member can benchmark itself against the observed distribution — exactly the peer-benchmark use case in the stem. SAMM is prescriptive-plus-self-assessment: it defines target activities and asks the organisation to score itself, without collecting data from other firms. Microsoft SDL is a prescriptive internal-Microsoft process describing what activities to perform in each SDLC phase, not a benchmark. ISO/IEC 27034 is a standards-track framework that specifies an Application Security Life Cycle and reusable Application Security Controls; it too is prescriptive rather than an observational benchmark.

questions.q: During requirements analysis for a new online-banking feature a security architect wants to write formal artefacts that describe how a hostile actor could try to interact with the system, so that counter-requirements (validation, rate limits, monitoring) can be derived alongside the normal user stories before any code is written. Which artefact is the architect producing?
choices: Misuse cases (also called abuse cases) — inverted use cases in which the actor has hostile intent, used during requirements to elicit counter-requirements.
Data-flow diagrams — element-and-edge diagrams that trace how data moves between processes, stores, and external entities across a trust boundary.
Security regression tests — automated checks that re-run against every build to confirm previously fixed vulnerabilities have not reappeared.
Non-functional requirements — quality attributes such as availability, performance, and maintainability that shape architecture but do not describe attackers.
questions.explanation: Misuse cases (Sindre and Opdahl, sometimes called abuse cases by McDermott and Fox) are the requirements-phase technique in which a use case is inverted: the actor becomes a malicious actor and the flow describes how the misuse is attempted, so the team can add mitigation requirements to the specification. Data-flow diagrams are the input to threat-modelling techniques like STRIDE, but they describe structure rather than an attacker's storyline. Security regression tests belong to the testing phase, long after requirements are frozen. Non-functional requirements capture quality attributes such as availability and performance; they do not describe an attacker's goals or actions.

questions.q: A design team is classifying a threat in which an attacker replays a captured session cookie against a web application because the cookie is not bound to a short-lived nonce or client fingerprint, allowing the attacker to impersonate a legitimate user for the rest of the session lifetime. In the STRIDE threat-model taxonomy, which category best describes this threat?
choices: Tampering — unauthorised modification of data or code either at rest or in transit that changes its content or meaning.
Repudiation — a user's ability to deny having performed an action because no reliable log or non-repudiable proof was recorded.
Spoofing identity — pretending to be a legitimate user or component by presenting stolen or forged credentials, tokens, or sessions.
Information disclosure — exposure of data to individuals not authorised to see it, such as verbose stack traces revealing internal state.
questions.explanation: Replaying a stolen session cookie lets the attacker act under another user's identity, which is the definition of the Spoofing identity category in STRIDE. Tampering would apply if the attacker modified the cookie's contents (for example, elevating a role claim) rather than presenting a legitimate but stolen cookie unchanged. Repudiation covers gaps in auditability that let a user later deny actions they performed; it does not describe presenting someone else's credentials. Information disclosure covers unintended read-side exposure of data (verbose errors, directory listing, insecure S3 buckets), not identity assumption.

nodes.title: Cryptography fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Crypto is the math layer that makes the rest of security possible. Most exam questions test symmetric vs asymmetric, hashing vs encryption, when to use which, and how key management actually works in practice.

flashcards.front: Symmetric vs asymmetric encryption — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Symmetric (AES-256, ChaCha20): one shared key, fast, used for bulk data. Asymmetric (RSA, ECC): public/private key pair, slow, used to exchange a symmetric key or to sign. Real systems use both: asymmetric to negotiate, symmetric to encrypt the bulk traffic (this is how TLS works).

flashcards.front: What's the difference between hashing and encryption?
flashcards.back: Encryption is reversible — the holder of the key can recover the plaintext. Hashing is one-way — you cannot derive the input from the output. Hashes are for integrity (did the file change?) and password storage (compare hashes, never store plaintext). SHA-256 is the modern default; MD5 and SHA-1 are broken.

A signature is a hash of the message encrypted with the signer's private key. Anyone with the public key can verify (decrypt the signature, recompute the hash, check they match). This proves authenticity (the holder of the private key signed it) AND integrity (the message wasn't tampered with).

flashcards.front: Why use a key management service (KMS)?
flashcards.back: Raw key handling is hard to do safely — you have to rotate, audit, restrict, destroy. A KMS holds keys in hardware, exposes encrypt/decrypt APIs, logs every use, enforces who can use which key. Your application code never sees the actual key material. AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP KMS all play this role.

questions.q: An architect designs a payment service so that even a fully compromised public web front-end still cannot reach the card-holder database directly — traffic must first pass through a hardened API gateway, then a WAF, then an authorisation service, and finally a network-restricted internal API before any query touches the database. No single control is trusted to be flawless. Which secure-design principle is being applied?
choices: Economy of mechanism — keep the design as small and simple as possible so it can be understood, reviewed, and reasoned about.
Complete mediation — every access to every object must be checked for authority every single time, with no cached bypass.
Fail-safe defaults — access decisions must default to deny and be granted only through explicit permit rules.
Defense in depth — layer multiple independent controls so that the compromise or bypass of a single one does not by itself grant access to the protected asset.
questions.explanation: Defense in depth is the design principle of stacking multiple independent controls so an attacker must defeat several of them in sequence to reach the protected asset, which is exactly the gateway → WAF → authorisation → internal API pattern described. Economy of mechanism is the opposite emphasis: minimise complexity so the design can be reviewed — it does not motivate stacking layers. Complete mediation requires that every access decision be re-checked at the enforcement point, but it does not by itself describe multiple stacked enforcement points. Fail-safe defaults dictate that missing rules deny access; that is a policy default, not the pattern of layered controls the scenario describes.

questions.q: A developer wants to eliminate SQL-injection risk in an Order-history endpoint that currently accepts an arbitrary customer_id string and interpolates it into a SELECT statement. The team must keep the same relational database and the same SQL query shape. Which mitigation should be adopted as the primary control?
choices: Escape single quotes in the input string with a custom sanitiser routine before concatenating it into the SQL text.
Use parameterised queries (prepared statements) so the customer_id travels to the database as a bound parameter rather than as part of the SQL text.
Deploy a web-application firewall in front of the endpoint with a SQL-injection signature rule set enabled in blocking mode.
Reject any input containing SQL keywords such as SELECT, UNION, DROP, or the ';' character using an allow-list regular expression.
questions.explanation: Parameterised queries (prepared statements) are the OWASP-recommended primary defence: the SQL text and the data are sent separately, so the database driver treats the customer_id as opaque data that can never be re-parsed as SQL. Custom quote-escaping routinely misses edge cases (Unicode variants, backslash escaping semantics, second-order injection) and is fragile; it is a well-known anti-pattern for this problem. A WAF is a useful additional layer but is a signature-based external control that can be bypassed with novel payloads, so it does not replace parameterisation as the primary fix. Keyword-blocking regular expressions block legitimate inputs (a customer whose name contains 'union') while still failing against encoded or fragmented payloads.

questions.q: A team is redesigning password storage for a new consumer service. They want a password-hashing scheme that is intentionally slow, memory-hard so custom-hardware attackers gain less advantage, side-channel resistant, and explicitly listed by OWASP as the preferred first choice for new applications in the current Password Storage Cheat Sheet. Which algorithm should they choose?
choices: Argon2id — a memory-hard, tunable, side-channel-resistant password hash that OWASP recommends as the first choice for new applications.
SHA-512 — a fast general-purpose cryptographic hash, typically salted per user record before storage.
bcrypt — a cost-tunable adaptive hash based on Blowfish, widely deployed but not memory-hard by construction.
PBKDF2 with SHA-256 at 10,000 iterations — a NIST-approved key-derivation function whose cost factor must be raised as hardware improves.
questions.explanation: Argon2id was the winner of the Password Hashing Competition and combines data-independent and data-dependent lookups, giving both memory hardness (which blunts GPU/ASIC crackers) and side-channel resistance. OWASP's Password Storage Cheat Sheet lists Argon2id as the first recommendation for new applications. Plain salted SHA-512 is far too fast — modern GPUs compute billions of hashes per second — and should never be used for passwords. bcrypt is an acceptable second choice and is legitimate for legacy environments, but it is not memory-hard, so it does not meet the memory-hardness requirement in the stem. PBKDF2 is FIPS-approved and acceptable when compliance requires it, but 10,000 iterations is well below current OWASP guidance and PBKDF2 is likewise not memory-hard.

questions.q: A pipeline engineer wants an automated security test that exercises the compiled application from the outside while it is running in a staging environment — sending crafted HTTP requests and analysing the responses to surface issues such as reflected cross-site scripting, open redirects, and insecure HTTP headers. No source code is provided to the test tool. Which technique fits the description?
choices: Static Application Security Testing (SAST) — analyses source, bytecode, or binaries at rest without executing the application.
Software Composition Analysis (SCA) — inventories third-party components in a build and matches their versions against known-vulnerability databases.
Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST) — probes a running application from the outside with crafted inputs and observes the resulting responses.
Interactive Application Security Testing (IAST) — instruments the running application with in-process agents that correlate incoming requests with dangerous internal sinks.
questions.explanation: DAST is defined by testing a live application from the outside via its exposed interfaces (typically HTTP), which matches the crafted-request / observe-response workflow described. SAST looks at source, bytecode, or binaries statically and does not need the application to be running; it also would need access to source or artefacts, which the scenario explicitly excludes. SCA inventories third-party dependencies against CVE databases; it does not exercise application endpoints. IAST also runs against a live application but requires an agent instrumenting the application from the inside — that inside visibility is what distinguishes it from the pure black-box DAST case in the stem.

nodes.title: Software supply-chain security: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Software supply-chain security protects everything that goes into building and delivering software — third-party dependencies, build pipelines, and published artifacts — because attackers increasingly compromise the supply chain instead of the app directly. Exams cover SBOMs, dependency risk, signing and provenance, and pipeline hardening.

flashcards.back: A Software Bill of Materials — a complete inventory of every component, library, and dependency in a piece of software, including versions. It lets you quickly answer 'are we affected?' when a new vulnerability (like Log4Shell) drops, instead of guessing what's inside your builds.

flashcards.front: What are typosquatting and poisoned dependencies?
flashcards.back: Typosquatting publishes a malicious package with a name nearly identical to a popular one (e.g., a one-letter difference), hoping you install it by mistake. A poisoned dependency is a legitimate package that's been compromised to inject malicious code into everyone who pulls it. Both attack you through trusted package ecosystems.

flashcards.front: What do artifact signing and provenance provide?
flashcards.back: Signing (e.g., with Sigstore/cosign) cryptographically proves an artifact came from a trusted publisher and wasn't tampered with. Provenance is verifiable metadata about how and where an artifact was built. Frameworks like SLSA define maturity levels for trustworthy, tamper-resistant build pipelines.

flashcards.front: How do you secure the CI/CD pipeline itself?
flashcards.back: Treat the pipeline as a high-value target: lock down build runners, scope credentials to least privilege and prefer short-lived tokens over stored secrets, pin and verify dependencies, isolate build steps, and require code review. A compromised build server can sign and ship malware as if it were legitimate.

questions.q: A team owns a native C library that parses a proprietary binary file format. They want to uncover memory-safety defects — buffer overflows, use-after-free, integer overflows — that only appear when the parser is fed unusual or malformed inputs the developers never anticipated. Which testing approach is best suited to that goal?
choices: Unit testing — small deterministic tests that exercise a single function against a curated set of expected inputs and outputs.
Regression testing — re-running previously passing tests to confirm no earlier defect has resurfaced after a change.
Behaviour-driven development (BDD) tests — Gherkin-style scenarios that express expected system behaviour in near-natural language.
Fuzz testing — feeding a large volume of randomised or mutated inputs to the parser and monitoring for crashes, hangs, or sanitiser errors.
questions.explanation: Fuzz testing (fuzzing) is purpose-built for exactly this goal: a fuzzer generates or mutates huge numbers of malformed inputs and watches for the crashes, hangs, or address/undefined-behaviour sanitiser trips that indicate memory-safety bugs in the parser. Unit tests exercise a narrow curated set of expected cases and are unlikely to hit the pathological inputs that trigger overflows. Regression tests re-run existing tests to catch resurfaced defects; they do not generate the novel inputs a fuzzer produces. BDD tests describe expected behaviour in human-readable scenarios and are also driven by planned inputs, not randomised or mutated ones.

questions.q: An audit finds that a microservice's production database password is baked into its config file, which is committed to a private Git repository and rendered into the container image at build time. Rotating the password now requires a new build and a redeploy. Which remediation best follows current secure-deployment practice?
choices: Move the password into a `.env` file that is added to `.gitignore` so it stops being committed to Git but continues to live inside the container image.

Store the password in a managed secrets store such as HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager and inject it into the running container at start-up via a short-lived token or dynamically issued credential.
Encrypt the config file with a symmetric key checked into the same repository as a separate file, so an attacker would need both files to recover the password.
Base64-encode the password inside the existing config file so a casual reader browsing the repository cannot immediately recognise it as a credential.
questions.explanation: The current best practice is to keep secrets out of source and out of images entirely: a managed secrets store holds the credential, the workload authenticates to that store with a short-lived identity (Vault AppRole, IAM role for service accounts, workload identity), and the secret is fetched at start-up or on-demand — enabling rotation without a rebuild and eliminating any static copy in the image. Moving the file into `.env`+`.gitignore` still bakes the credential into the image and does not enable rotation. Encrypting the file with a key stored beside it defeats the purpose because whoever can read the repository can read both files. Base64 is not encryption — it is a trivially reversible encoding — and provides no confidentiality against any attacker.

questions.q: A medical-device regulator asks the vendor to provide a machine-readable inventory of every open-source and third-party component (with versions, suppliers, and licences) that ships inside the firmware, so downstream operators can react quickly when a new CVE is disclosed against any of those components. Which artefact satisfies this requirement?
choices: A Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) exported in an interoperable format such as CycloneDX or SPDX, listing components, versions, suppliers, and their relationships.
A threat model in STRIDE-per-element form describing each asset in the design and the classes of threat that apply to it.
A penetration-test report enumerating the exploitable weaknesses discovered during the most recent black-box engagement against the device.
A screenshot of the vendor's software-composition-analysis dashboard exported from the internal build server.
questions.explanation: A Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) is precisely the machine-readable component inventory the regulator is asking for; CycloneDX and SPDX are the two industry-standard interoperable formats and are the ones cited by NTIA / CISA / the FDA pre-market cybersecurity guidance. A threat model expresses risk, not component identity. A penetration-test report enumerates weaknesses observed during a single engagement and cannot be re-queried when tomorrow's CVE lands. An SCA dashboard screenshot is neither machine-readable nor an interoperable artefact — it also captures only the vendor's internal view rather than the deliverable format the regulator can ingest.

questions.q: A platform team wants to guarantee that any container image deployed to production was built by their trusted CI pipeline from a known source commit, and that nothing in transit or in the registry has been swapped for a malicious substitute before the workload starts. Which control most directly satisfies that goal?
choices: Enable vulnerability scanning of the image at pull time and block deployment if any Critical CVE is present in the scan result.
Move the registry inside the private network and restrict pull access with IAM policies that only production nodes can assume.
Sign the image at build time (for example with Sigstore Cosign) and configure the runtime to admit only images whose signature and SLSA provenance attestation verify against the trusted key.
Rebuild the image locally on every deployment target from the source repository so no upstream tampering can persist between build and run.
questions.explanation: Signing the artefact at build time and verifying that signature (plus a provenance attestation that ties the artefact back to the pipeline and source commit) at admission is the direct integrity-and-provenance control the scenario asks for; SLSA levels 2–3 and Sigstore/Cosign are the canonical implementations. Vulnerability scanning finds known CVEs in the content but says nothing about who built the image or whether it was tampered with. Registry access controls limit who can push or pull, but a compromised registry insider — or a mis-routed pull — could still serve a substituted image; admission then has no way to notice. Local rebuild on every target is operationally impractical and moves rather than removes the trust problem: something still has to attest that the local rebuild used the intended source.
